title: Frequently asked questions about Medicare
summary: Common questions and answers about Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Part D, Medicare Supplement, eligibility, working past 65, enrollment periods, costs, and choosing a plan.

atoms.title: What Original Medicare is
atoms.question: What is Original Medicare?
atoms.text: Original Medicare consists of Medicare Part A (hospital coverage) and Medicare Part B (medical coverage). It's a federal health insurance program for individuals 65 or older; under 65 who have a qualifying disability; and of any age with a diagnosis of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS, also called Lou Gehrig's disease).

atoms.title: What Medicare Part A covers
atoms.question: What does Medicare Part A cover?
atoms.text: Medicare Part A covers hospital charges and most associated services while you are admitted as an inpatient. Coverage includes a semi-private room, hospital meals, skilled nursing services, care on special units such as intensive care, drugs, supplies and equipment used during your stay, lab tests and X-rays, operating and recovery room services, some blood transfusions, rehab through home health care, skilled care in your home if you are homebound and need only part-time care, and hospice care. Part B covers doctor visits, even in the hospital, and outpatient services.

atoms.title: Medicare versus Medicaid
atoms.question: Is Medicare the same as Medicaid?
atoms.text: No. Medicare and Medicaid are both government programs that help people pay for health care, but they are not the same. Medicare is a federal program that provides coverage for people who are 65 or older or have certain qualifying disabilities. Medicaid is a joint state and federal program that provides coverage for individuals and families with limited incomes. Dual eligibility means you qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid.

atoms.title: Whether Medicare is mandatory
atoms.question: Is Medicare mandatory?
atoms.text: No. Medicare is not mandatory. But if you do decide to enroll after your Initial Enrollment Period and don't qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you could face late enrollment penalties for Medicare Part A, Part B, Part C or Part D.

atoms.title: Prescription drugs under Original Medicare
atoms.question: Can I get my prescription drugs covered under Original Medicare?
atoms.text: No. Original Medicare doesn't generally cover prescription drugs, though Part A may cover some drugs you get as an inpatient. Part D coverage is available separately through private insurers approved by Medicare, either as a standalone plan or in a Medicare Advantage plan with drug benefits. All Part D plans have a drug list (formulary) showing which drugs are covered; the formulary can change, and your plan will let you know ahead of time.

atoms.title: Choosing doctors and referrals under Medicare
atoms.question: Can I choose my doctor? Does Medicare require referrals?
atoms.text: Your choice of doctor depends on what Medicare coverage you have. With Original Medicare (Part A and Part B) you can see any doctor that accepts Medicare. Most Medicare Advantage plans have provider networks, and some plans may require referrals to specialists. Both Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage plans cover most emergency care when and where it's needed.

atoms.title: Dental, vision and hearing under Original Medicare
atoms.question: Does Original Medicare cover vision, dental, or hearing care?
atoms.text: Generally, no. Original Medicare doesn't cover routine vision or dental care, eyeglasses or hearing aids. Part B may cover some dental or vision services if you meet certain conditions and they are considered medically necessary, but check with your provider and Medicare first. Many Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans do offer these benefits, including routine eye exams with eyeglasses and corrective lenses, dental exams, and hearing tests and hearing aids.

atoms.title: Nursing home stays under Original Medicare
atoms.question: Does Original Medicare pay for a nursing home stay?
atoms.text: Original Medicare Part A pays for some skilled nursing services, but doesn't cover long-term or custodial care for daily life activities like eating and bathing. You would also still be responsible for a portion of the costs, such as deductibles, copays and coinsurance.

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage HMO versus PPO
atoms.question: What's the difference between a Medicare Advantage HMO and PPO?
atoms.text: A Medicare Advantage HMO plan usually helps pay only for care you receive from providers in the plan network. A PPO plan will generally help pay for care received outside the plan network, but it may pay less than for the same care received within the network.

atoms.title: Medicare Advantage versus Medicare Supplement
atoms.question: What's the difference between a Medicare Advantage plan and a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: A Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan combines Part A, Part B, and often Part D drug coverage in one plan, may include benefits like hearing, vision, dental and fitness, and has an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs on covered services. A Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan helps with some out-of-pocket costs that Original Medicare doesn't pay, like coinsurance and copayments. You can have either a Medicare Advantage plan or a Medicare Supplement plan, but not both at the same time.

atoms.title: Medigap open enrollment and guaranteed issue
atoms.question: When can I apply for Medicare Supplement insurance?
atoms.text: The best time to enroll in a Medicare Supplement plan is during your Medicare Supplement Open Enrollment period because acceptance is guaranteed. It starts on the first day of the month in which you are both age 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. Some states have additional Open Enrollment periods and Guaranteed Issue requirements. If you apply outside these periods, you may be denied coverage or charged more based on your health history, except in Connecticut and New York, where open enrollment and guaranteed issue is ongoing.

atoms.title: Special Enrollment Period for life events
atoms.question: What is a Medicare Special Enrollment Period?
atoms.text: Medicare grants a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) when you are working past 65 with creditable coverage from your employer and for certain qualifying life events. The SEP for working past 65 gives eight months to enroll in Part A and Part B, but only the first two months to get a Medicare Advantage (Part C) and Part D plan without penalty. A separate 2-month SEP exists for people who already have Medicare and have a qualifying life event, such as moving to a state where their Medicare Advantage plan is not offered.

atoms.title: Automatic renewal and the Annual Notice of Change
atoms.question: Do I have to change plans every year or can I keep the same one?
atoms.text: If there are no changes to the contract or coverage area associated with your provider, your Medicare coverage should renew automatically, although plan benefits and costs may change even if a plan renews. You don't have to change plans, but you should always check your options. Review the Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) your insurer sends each fall, which lists any changes in plan coverage, costs, or service areas, and review choices during the Annual Enrollment Period from October 15 to December 7.

atoms.title: Costs of Original Medicare
atoms.question: How much does Original Medicare Part A and Part B cost?
atoms.text: Most people pay no premium for Medicare Part A. The premium for Medicare Part B depends on your income and may change each year. For both Part A and Part B there are also deductibles and coinsurance. With Original Medicare you will pay 20% coinsurance based on the Medicare-approved amount, including for inpatient care and durable medical equipment like a wheelchair or CPAP machine. Many Medicare Advantage plans also have a 20% coinsurance payment for certain services.

atoms.title: Financial help paying for Medicare
atoms.question: Can I get financial help to pay for Medicare?
atoms.text: Financial assistance programs for people with limited income and assets include Extra Help for prescription drugs, Medicare Savings Programs and Medicaid. Program requirements and levels of support will vary. Extra Help is also called Low Income Subsidy (LIS), and a Dual Special Needs plan (D-SNP) is a Medicare Advantage plan with drug coverage for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid.

atoms.title: Where to compare plans and get free help
atoms.question: Where else can I compare Medicare plans, and what if I get overwhelmed?
atoms.text: The plan comparison page at Medicare.gov shows options from all providers, and you can compare 2027 plans available where you live, with results for premiums, projected drug spend, out-of-pocket costs and added benefits. You can also create a My Medicare account. For help, you can get answers from Medicare.gov or from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), which provides free Medicare help from trained counselors.
